text.gc1: Almost all data travels in cables.
text.gc2: But a ship's anchor can cut one.
text.gc3: No problem. There are many cables, so it takes another way.
text.h1: At her end, a tower turns the light back into radio.
text.e1: That took less than a blink.
text.e2: But how do we know the photo is exactly the same?
text.g1: Almost all data between continents travels in cables like this.
text.g2: Our photo crosses from Hyderabad to London.
text.m1: But three are missing. Her phone asks for them again.
text.a1: On her phone, the pieces land in any order.
text.a2: The numbers put them back in line.
text.a3: Her phone decrypts them, and the photo appears.
text.a4: About 65 milliseconds. Faster than a blink.
text.c1: The cable is thin, about as thick as a garden hose.
text.c2: Steel wires and plastic protect it from anchors and sea water.
text.c3: A copper tube carries power to the repeaters.
text.c4: In the middle, glass fibres, thin as a hair.
text.q1: Three kilometres down, in the Arabian Sea, the photo is only light.
text.q2: Light in glass travels about 200,000 kilometres every second.
text.q3: As it fades, a repeater, every 60 to 100 kilometres, boosts it.
text.r1: At the next stop, a router reads the label. Each router only knows the next step.
text.r2: If a road is busy, it sends it another way.
text.r3: Then the land ends. The cable goes into the sea.
text.r4: From here, it all travels as light, under the sea.
